1.pericope_label: O sing unto the Lord a new song, for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand and his holy arm hath gotten him the victory

schools.summary: Augustine makes the new song the property of the new man, the old life being derived from Adam and the new formed in Christ, and argues that those who cut themselves off from the communion of the whole earth cannot sing it, since it is sung in the whole and not in a part; he takes the holy arm and the right hand for the Lord himself rather than for a figure of his power.

Calvin begins from the psalm’s resemblance to an earlier one in matter and language, and presses the manner of the deliverance: the praise called for is extraordinary and not common because the salvation was singular and wrought without human means, ordinary means taking nothing from the glory of God but keeping us from discovering his presence so fully. Gill keeps to a short note, an excellent song for the redemption wrought and the new and living way opened.

Henry makes the song new by its subject, a praise for redeeming love such as had not been sung before, and observes that converts change their wonder and their joy and therefore their note, so that grace which puts a new heart in the breast puts a new song in the mouth, while in the new Jerusalem the songs will be new to eternity; he has the victory won by the Redeemer’s own power and won not for himself only but for us. Spurgeon dates the newness, a song before because the Lord was coming and another now because he has come and conquered, and finds the wonder in the inadequacy of the means, since idols fell and systems of error fled before a moral and not a physical power.

Clarke collects the titles the versions give the psalm, a bare psalm in the Hebrew, a prophetic psalm in one, a psalm of David in three others, and in another an ascription to David referring it to the restoration from Egypt but bidding it be understood spiritually of the advent of the Messiah and the calling of the Gentiles; his own guess is that it was written for the deliverance from the Babylonish captivity and is to be read prophetically of the redemption of the world; and he reports that the clause rendered victory says literally that he has made salvation for himself.

Keil and Delitzsch note that this is the only psalm inscribed with the single word psalm, for which a rabbinic tractate calls it the orphan psalm, deny that the new song is the song of Moses and make it rather its counterpart, and observe that the opening and close are borrowed from an earlier psalm while almost everything between comes from the later chapters of Isaiah, a book that has become as it were a spring for religious song. Ellicott notes in one line that the word rendered victory is more commonly rendered salvation.

debates: Is the new song the song of Moses? Keil and Delitzsch say it is rather the counterpart of that song, since what resounded for the first time at the sea is here sung as a completion, and they set aside the old version that heads the psalm as concerning the redemption out of Egypt.

What occasion produced the psalm? Clarke guesses the deliverance from the Babylonish captivity and reads it prophetically of the redemption of the world; Keil and Delitzsch derive its language from an earlier psalm and from the later chapters of Isaiah.

What is the holy arm? Augustine takes it for the Lord himself rather than a figure of his power, while Clarke reduces the clause to its Hebrew, that he has made salvation for himself, and Ellicott observes that the word rendered victory is usually rendered salvation.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report that a rabbinic tractate calls this the orphan psalm because its inscription carries no further word.
Keil and Delitzsch call the later chapters of Isaiah a spring for religious song, since almost everything between this psalm’s borrowed opening and close is drawn from them.
Spurgeon finds the victory the more wonderful for the inadequacy of its means, a moral rather than a physical power.
themes: a psalm with no name to it
the old man and the new song
victory or salvation in one word

2.pericope_label: The Lord hath made known his salvation: he hath remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel: make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all the earth: sing unto the Lord with the harp

schools.summary: Henry treats the passage as a coronation, the King welcomed to the throne with acclamations and loud shouts till the earth ring again, as when Solomon was proclaimed, and the harp reinforced by trumpet and cornet because the King is victorious; he guards it by calling carnal mirth an enemy to holy joy and recalling that David danced before the ark and pleaded that it was before the Lord. Spurgeon demands that every tongue applaud with the vigour which joy of heart alone can arouse, borrows a direction from Wesley to sing lustily and beware of singing as if half dead, and yet insists the song come from the heart, since otherwise the music is only a noise in the ears of God.

Gill distinguishes the salvation wrought from the salvation published, unknown to the Gentile world until the everlasting Gospel made it known and a spirit of revelation gave some to know their own interest in it; and he refuses the instruments of the fifth verse as an allusion to the older worship, holding that the newer worship is expressed in the older language and that harps in the hands of the saints mean nothing but spiritual melody in their hearts.

Clarke puts the emphasis on the manner of the deliverance, so wrought as to show that it was supernatural and that confidence in the unseen God had not been in vain, takes the mercy remembered for the promise made to the forefathers and the truth for the keeping of it, and doubts that the word translated psalm means a psalm at all, taking it for a musical instrument or a species of ode modulated by different voices. Wesley says the redemption was hitherto reserved and not thoroughly known even by most of the people who kept the promise, and reads the righteousness as the faithfulness that accomplished it.

Keil and Delitzsch read the summons as a call for joyful manifestation of the mouth, which may be done in many ways, and find the verses adding first song with stringed instruments as of the Levites and then wind instruments as of the priests, noting that the language throughout echoes earlier psalms and prophets. Ellicott would render the first summons as a breaking out into songs and music and the second as playing to the Lord on a harp with melodious sound.

debates: Are the instruments of the fifth verse to be used now? Gill denies it, taking them for the older worship expressed in the older language and reducing harps to spiritual melody in the heart, while Henry and Spurgeon call for trumpet and cornet and for the loudest praise the throat can give.

What does the word translated psalm mean? Clarke doubts the common rendering and takes it for either a musical instrument or a species of ode modulated by different voices; Ellicott renders the clause as melodious sound of music.
How far may the noise go? Spurgeon allows every form of exultation but insists the song come from the heart, and Henry warns that carnal mirth is an enemy to holy joy.
outliers: Spurgeon quotes Wesley by name in this psalm, borrowing his direction to sing lustily and with good courage, so that two of the voices in the set meet on the page.
Keil and Delitzsch distribute the instruments by office, strings to the Levites and winds to the priests.
Henry compares the welcome of the King to the proclamation of Solomon, when the shouting made the earth ring again.
themes: a coronation shout for a victorious King
strings for the Levites, winds for the priests
harps in the hand or melody in the heart
singing lustily and singing from the heart

6.pericope_label: With trumpets and sound of cornet make a joyful noise before the Lord, the King: let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof: let the floods clap their hands: for he cometh to judge the earth

schools.summary: Spurgeon refuses to reduce the sea to a figure for nations, holding that it should not be denied a place in the orchestra of nature, that its thunders are not too grand for the theme and that a great composer of choruses would have been glad of its aid, its deep bass suiting the mystery of the divine glory; he sets sacred song above the classical, since the muses of Parnassus cannot rival the muse of Zion and the Castalian fount never sparkled like the fount of every blessing; and he quotes the same lines on the live thunder that Ellicott quotes, without naming their author.

Gill begins to report how three old versions render the instruments of the sixth verse and his note breaks off before he says what they make of it; he calls the clapping of the floods a prosopopoeia and reports a rabbinic interpreter who took the sea for those in ships, the rivers for the men in them, and the hills for those who dwell upon them.

Clarke admits he knows nothing of the form or management of the first instrument named and identifies the second as the ordinary word for a trumpet; he takes the roaring sea for poetic imagery or for maritime and commercial nations, the rivers for continents where only large rivers are found so that inland peoples are included, and the hills for the inhabitants of mountainous countries; and he devotes his longest note to a comparison of the psalm with the song of the mother of the Lord, printing five pairs in two columns after a bishop’s parallels and calling David the Voice and Mary the Echo.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the clapping rivers are original to this psalm, the waves flowing into one another as hands are struck together. Ellicott notes that the sixth verse is the only place in the psalm where the straight trumpet appears, hears the lapping of waves in the clapping of the floods and finds the expression in one of the prophets, and quotes two poets, one on the mighty Being awake whose eternal motion sounds like thunder and one on the live thunder leaping from peak to peak.

debates: Do the sea, the floods and the hills stand for nature or for peoples? Clarke reads them as maritime nations, inland continents and mountain dwellers, and Gill reports a rabbinic interpreter who does the same, while Spurgeon insists the sea itself belongs in the orchestra of nature and Ellicott keeps to the sound of the waves.

What is the clapping of the floods? Keil and Delitzsch make it waves flowing into one another as hands are struck together and call the image original to this psalm; Ellicott hears the lapping sound of waves and finds the expression in one of the prophets.

What is the psalm ultimately about? Clarke argues from its parallels with the song of the mother of the Lord that whatever deliverance it records, it is to be understood of the redemption of the world.
outliers: Clarke prints the psalm and the song of the mother of the Lord in two columns, five pairs deep, calling David the Voice and Mary the Echo.
Ellicott and Spurgeon independently quote the same four lines on the live thunder leaping from peak to peak; Ellicott names the poet and the poem, Spurgeon does not.
Gill’s note on the sixth verse breaks off in the middle of a sentence, after naming three old versions but before reporting their rendering.
themes: the sea as nation or as orchestra
mountains given a tongue by the poets
